lines: Same question, asked two ways against the exact same system, both measured directly.
One version scans every single raw record from the very beginning, every single time it's asked.
The other version is handed a table that already holds the answer — and comes back dramatically faster, watched directly rather than assumed.
Worth reasoning through before settling on an answer.
Both versions of this question ran against the exact same underlying system, with nothing swapped out underneath.
So is the fast one fast because it's secretly a fundamentally different kind of system, or because it's simply being asked a much smaller question than the slow one?
answer: It's the smaller question — nothing about the system itself changed.
The real work of combining all those records into one answer already happened once, ahead of time.
What's left to scan on the fast path is tiny by comparison, which is the entire reason it comes back quickly.

lines: Here's what that ahead-of-time work actually is, and isn't.
None of the real combining work disappears — it still has to happen somewhere.
What changes is when it happens: once, the moment new data arrives, instead of being redone from scratch every single time someone asks the question.
Here's that exact comparison, with real numbers behind it rather than just a description.
A table built ahead of time, holding the combined answer already, is measured directly against the raw version it came from.
It answers the identical question many times faster, confirmed to give the exact same result either way.
Here's the real cost that speed carries, measured rather than just claimed.
A brand-new record is added to the raw version, and checking the raw version again immediately shows it, right away.
Checking the pre-built answer immediately afterward, though, measurably does not show that new record — not until that pre-built version is explicitly rebuilt.
One more idea, worth naming on its own.
A single pre-built answer only ever answers the one question it was built for.

A broader structure instead precomputes every combination across a chosen handful of categories at once, trading a lot more storage for being ready for any question drawn from those categories, not just a single one.
A handful of real, named systems take this idea one step further than anything described so far.
Instead of combining records later, on a schedule, they do that combining the instant each record first arrives.
And their own documentation is upfront about the real price of that: once something's been combined this way, you can no longer go back and ask about that one original record by itself.
Pulling the whole topic back together.
Combining data ahead of time doesn't remove the work; it just moves when that work happens, to the moment data is written.

A pre-built answer is measurably faster, but that speed can come with the real cost of staleness until it's rebuilt. A broader structure generalizes one pre-built answer into many at once. And some real systems push that same idea all the way back to the instant data first arrives.
One closing scenario, worth reasoning through before the explanation lands.
Something needs to show a number that's correct down to the second, while being asked for constantly — far too often to recompute from the full raw records every time.
Of everything named in this topic, which approach actually fits, and what does choosing it really cost?
answer: The systems that combine data the instant it arrives, not on any kind of schedule.
A table rebuilt only periodically is never fresher than its last rebuild, and scanning every raw record directly isn't affordable at that request volume.
The real cost isn't the technique itself — it's standing up and running an entire extra, dedicated system just to get it.
